how does "requires oAuth" jibe with my ability to write to the gsheet in an incognito browser window without being logged in to google?
16:49 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 1m16s · 1m20s wall-clock time

Great question — it's the exact confusion the README should preempt, so I'll answer and then tighten the doc.

The reconciliation: you're walking through two different doors.

When you edit in an incognito window, you're using *Google's own Sheets frontend*. For a sheet set to "anyone with the link can edit," the link itself is the credential — a capability URL. The docs app mints an anonymous session for you behind the scenes (that's why you show up as "Anonymous Wombat" in the presence indicators — you *do* have a session, just not an account), and it talks to Google's private, undocumented sync endpoints using its own cookies and XSRF tokens. That machinery is first-party only.

The public API at sheets.googleapis.com is a separate door with a different bouncer. It has no concept of an anonymous principal: every write request must carry an OAuth token identifying *some* account, and only then does Google check whether that account has edit rights under the sharing settings. "Anyone with the link can edit" never enters the picture, because the request dies at authentication, before authorization is even considered — hence the 401 CREDENTIALS_MISSING we saw, not a 403. API keys don't bridge the gap either: they identify a billing project, not a person, so Google restricts them to reads of public data.

Could you, in principle, replicate what the incognito browser does — grab anonymous session cookies and speak the private protocol? Yes, technically, but it's undocumented, brittle, bot-protected, and changes without notice. Not a foundation to build on. So the practical statement stands: *third-party code* can't write without OAuth, and the Apps Script is the cheapest way to be a first party.

I've updated the appendix to bake this in, since it's the obvious "wait, but…" for anyone following the recipe:

TL;DR: two different doors. Your incognito edit goes through Google's own Sheets frontend, where the link itself acts as the credential — the app mints an anonymous session behind the scenes (hence "Anonymous Wombat" in the presence bar; you *have* a session, just not an account) and talks to private, first-party-only endpoints. The public API at sheets.googleapis.com is a separate door with no concept of an anonymous principal: every write must carry an OAuth token identifying *some* account. Requests without one die at authentication — which is why we got a 401 (CREDENTIALS_MISSING) rather than a 403 — before your generous sharing settings are ever consulted. API keys don't bridge it either: they identify a billing project, not a person, and are read-only by design.

Could code imitate the browser — scrape anonymous session cookies and speak the undocumented sync protocol? Technically yes, practically no: brittle, bot-protected, changes without notice. So "requires OAuth" really means "requires OAuth *for anything you'd want to build on*," and the Apps Script is the cheapest way to be a first party.

Since this is the obvious "wait, but…" for anyone following the recipe, I baked the reconciliation into the README: the appendix's "The problem" section now explains the anonymous-session story explicitly, and the Architecture section says "*programmatic* writes" and points to the appendix. 18:58 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 1m27s · 1m29s wall-clock time

That error is Google's plumbing failing, not anything you did wrong — and I have a strong suspicion about the cause. Behind the scenes, every Apps Script project gets a hidden Google Cloud project with an auto-generated OAuth client, and invalid_client: The OAuth client was not found means the consent flow looked up that client in the wrong account context. The classic trigger: being signed into multiple Google accounts at once — and the error screen says dreeves@gmail.com while your primary is presumably dreeves@beeminder.com, so you're almost certainly multi-logged-in, and the Apps Script editor is infamous for exactly this failure under multi-login (the editor session runs under one account while the consent popup resolves under the other).

In order of likelihood of fixing it:

  1. Match the accounts. Look at the avatar in the top-right of the Apps Script editor to see which account the editor is actually running as. Re-run authorize and, at the account chooser, pick *exactly that* account.
  2. If that fails, eliminate multi-login: open the sheet in an incognito window (or a browser profile) signed into *only one* account, Extensions → Apps Script, run authorize there. This is the reliable fix.
  3. Check the GCP association: gear icon (Project Settings) → "Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Project" should say *Default*. If a custom project is attached, its OAuth client is gone/misconfigured — simplest recovery is a fresh script project (re-paste the code).
  4. Rarely it's propagation lag on a brand-new script project — waiting a few minutes and retrying fixes it.

One reassurance: since the sheet is world-editable, it doesn't matter *which* of your accounts ends up authorizing — whichever account deploys with "Execute as: Me" becomes the writer, and both of yours can write. The only requirement is that the consent account matches the editor's account.

Let me bake this into the README's troubleshooting so future-you doesn't re-debug it:

TL;DR: you're multi-logged-in, and the Apps Script editor hates that. Error 401: invalid_client means the consent popup looked up the script's auto-generated OAuth client under the wrong account context — note the error names dreeves@gmail.com while you're presumably usually dreeves@beeminder.com. Your code is fine; nothing is misconfigured on your end.

To get past it, in order of likelihood:

  1. Check the avatar in the Apps Script editor's top-right corner to see which account the *editor* is running as, re-run authorize, and pick exactly that account in the chooser.
  2. If it still fails: incognito window signed into just one account → open the sheet → Extensions → Apps Script → run authorize. This is the reliable fix.
  3. Long shots: Project Settings (gear) → GCP project should say "Default"; and brand-new script projects occasionally need a few minutes before auth works.

Since the sheet is world-editable, it genuinely doesn't matter which of your two accounts ends up owning the deployment — whichever deploys with "Execute as: Me" becomes the writer.

Challenge accepted — hunting by adversarial inspection of every async/edge path, then proving kills with quals. Two candidates found by reading:

Bug 1 (nasty): clear the "Reveal after [n]" field while retyping it — the input fires, the 700ms debounce elapses while the field is empty, parseInt('') → NaN → Math.max(1, NaN||1) → 1, and the app pushes n=1… which instantly force-reveals a live auction. A transient UI state performs the most destructive action in the system.

Bug 2 (race): submit a bid, then switch auctions while the POST is in flight — the response handler stores your bid in localStorage under the *new* auction's key (module-level aname changed mid-flight), so your own bid shows on the wrong auction and masks on the right one.

Proving both red before fixing:

Bug 1 red confirmed (bug 2's assertions sit after the crash point — both get fixed now):

Two bugs found, both killed red→green. All 166 assertions pass.

Bug 1 — blank n force-reveals. Replicata: auction sealed at 1 of 2 bids; select-all the "Reveal after [2]" field to retype it as 3; pause ~a second. Expectata: nothing happens until you type a number. Resultata: the debounce fired on the empty field, parseInt('') → NaN, the old Math.max(1, NaN || 1) silently "fixed" it to 1, and the auction irreversibly revealed. Classic anti-Postel violation — the silent clamp was the bug. Fix: pushSettings now holds fire unless the field parses to a number ≥ 1 (one new if-statement, disclosed); the clamp is gone. Residual edge, also disclosed: typing "10" and pausing more than 700ms after the "1" still legitimately pushes n=1 — the debounce covers normal typing speed, and n=1 is a value users may genuinely want, so it can't be forbidden outright.

Bug 2 — bid attributed to the wrong auction. Replicata: submit a bid, then switch auctions within ~500ms while the POST is in flight. Expectata: your bid is remembered under the auction it was placed on. Resultata: the response handler read the module-level aname — already changed — and stored your bid under the *new* auction: readable on the wrong page, masked on the right one. Fix: placeBid pins the auction at submit time and uses it for the request and the storage key (the render guard still compares against the live value, correctly). The qual simulates the race with injectable mock latency.

Places I audited and found clean, for the record: every other use of aname after an await (refresh and pushSettings are guarded), repaint row indexing in Code.gs, corrupted-localStorage behavior (throws loudly, by design), the chip-remove/blur event interplay, uppercase and trailing-slash URLs, and double-submit during flight (button disabled).

Thought it through against the real use cases. Here's where I landed:

The root flaw: auto-join made the roster mean "whoever showed up," but auto-reveal still treats it as "everyone we're expecting" — so the moment two drive-by bidders exist, "everyone has bid" is trivially true and the latch detonates. Any design that keeps *automatic* reveal has to guess when the group is complete, and a wrong guess is irreversible by your own (correct) latch invariant. The asymmetry decides it: a wrong auto-reveal is catastrophic and permanent; an extra tap on a button is nothing. So: reveal becomes a human act — your button idea — and auto-reveal dies entirely. Walking the cases:

  • *Ad-hoc group* (your scenario): alice and bob bid rosterlessly → roster builds itself → nothing reveals until someone says so. Fixed.
  • *Organizer flow* (the sealedbids model): roster set upfront, last bid arrives → button lights up in everyone's window → any participant taps it. One tap of friction buys never-wrong reveals.
  • *Straggler*: today, removing a chip *detonates the reveal as a side effect* — surprising even when intended. With a button, roster edits never reveal anything by themselves.
  • *Solo/tester*: button stays dark below two bidders ("an auction takes two" survives).
  • The latch, permissive edits, auto-join seating, and late-public-bids all stay exactly as they are; the server just moves the latch-write into a new reveal action that anyone may call.

Roster-commitment-first (the Slack-faithful alternative) solves the same problem but taxes every auction to fix the sloppy ones — drive-by bidding is this web version's whole charm. I'd reject it.

On killing the word "reveal": the padlock badge can *become* the button — a grayed 🔒 that starts breathing when conditions are met, and pressing it pops it open to 🔓 with the tada. State and action collapse into one wordless element. (Discoverability is the risk; your tooltip pattern covers it.)

Click-your-name makes identity a pick instead of a re-type — typo-proof by construction.

Here's the shape that I think hangs together:

The three boxes become: auction name → Roster → BIDS. The YOU field, BID field, and submit button disappear. In the BIDS list, an empty row is a bid slot: tap your name, the row expands into an inline input ("your bid, @bob" as placeholder), enter or a small in-row ✓ submits (the ✓ matters on mobile — can't rely on the keyboard's enter). Your own green row stays editable the same way for re-bids; the placeholder-shows-your-old-bid trick migrates into the row. Padlock, counters, shimmer, stacked cards all stay where they are — the whole game now lives in one box, which makes the padlock-on-the-BIDS-box design even more coherent.

The identity crux. You can't enforce one-person-one-device without auth, and the app already doesn't — the YOU field is exactly as spoofable today. So the goal is making the *default path* say "pick yourself, once," and I'd do it with a latch: first inline bid sets tauction-uname (which already exists and is global); from then on, only your row is interactive — other empty rows render inert, no hover affordance, no cursor change. Your row gets a small "(you)" marker plus a quiet "not @alice?" escape hatch that clears the latch. Before the latch, every empty row is tappable, and the act of typing in a row *is* the claim "this is me" — the placeholder makes that legible. This also leaves the shelved pass-the-device case technically possible (clear, bid, clear, bid) but frictioned, which matches "shouldn't" rather than "can't."

The one real design decision: drive-by bidders. Today a non-roster person can bid via the form and joins publicly. With no form, they need a path. Two options: (a) a ghost row at the bottom of the BIDS list — blank name + blank bid, basically the old form reincarnated as a row, which also saves the rosterless-new-auction case from being a dead end; or (b) no ghost row — outsiders add themselves in the Roster box first, then their row appears. I lean (b): it's one less row-state, it matches the roster-only model you already committed to, and the Roster box is sitting right there. The cost is that a brand-new auction requires touching the roster before anyone can bid — which is arguably the correct ritual anyway ("name the participants and point everyone at the URL").

One tension to flag: once bids rows are the interaction surface, the Roster box and the BIDS box display the same people twice, and the duplication gets more visible. The endgame of your idea is probably merging them — roster editing as add/remove on the bids rows themselves. I'd *not* do that now: roster editing is a shared settings action while bidding is personal, and mixing both affordances into one row multiplies states. Keep the Roster box this round; merge later if the duplication grates.

Costs: a substantial app.js and quals rewrite (frontend-quals and story-quals lean heavily on #uname/#bid/submit), zero GAS redeploy, and honestly *more* UI state in JS than today — the simplification is entirely in what the user sees, which I think is the point. Yes — and this merge is the Saint-Exupéry move, because it doesn't just combine two boxes, it deletes one entirely. The app becomes: auction name, one ledger, footer. Let me take your three questions in turn.

× on rows — your instinct is right, and the semantics already agree. The only *real* purpose removal serves is unblocking the padlock (your end-early flow: ex the straggler, press reveal). Only people who haven't bid ever block it, so × on a green row has no job to do. Better: it *can't* do its apparent job — bids live in the bids tab and bidding claims a roster seat, so exing a bidder today just leaves them struck-through with their bid intact; in the merged UI that × would read as "delete this sealed bid," which must never be a thing (that's a cheat button: suppress a rival's bid before reveal). So the rule is: × appears only on rows with no bid, and removing one deletes the row outright. Pleasing consequence — the struck-through state becomes unreachable, so the cut class, the rejoin-on-rebid logic, and their quals can all be deleted. The simplification compounds.

Which one is you. Carry over the latch from last round: first inline bid sets tauction-uname, and from then on your row is the only interactive one. The identity marker is then mostly *the affordance itself* — your row is the one that invites typing — reinforced by a subtle accent edge and a small "(you)" tag with a quiet "not you?" release next to it. Before anyone's latched, no row is "you" yet, and that's honest: on a fresh device, tapping a name and bidding *is* the claim. A returning device pre-marks your row since tauction-uname is global. I'd resist the temptation to float your row to the top — everyone seeing the same order keeps the ledger shared-reality, which matters when people are pointing at screens.

The + row. Bottom of the list, expands to a name input. It serves all three adders with one affordance: the initiator naming participants, someone adding a forgotten person, and a drive-by adding themself (which resolves last round's open question — roster-first wins by default, because the roster UI is now inside the bids box anyway). Hide + and × after reveal, matching the everything-locks rule. Under the hood + and × are just saveSettings roster writes and bidding is placeBid — Code.gs and the sheet schema are untouched; this is still a frontend-only change.

  2. Row-state count. One box, but each row now has ~6 states (empty/tappable, empty/inert-with-×, yours-editable, green-masked, green-yours, revealed) plus the + row. Fewer things on screen, more states in app.js, and a substantial frontend-quals/story-quals rewrite. I think that trade is exactly the point — but it's where the complexity went, not vanished.

Yes — a participants table is the right structure, and the claims table was a deliberately thin slice of exactly that. But the interesting part of your question isn't the rename; it's the semantics that come with it.

What "users table" actually buys. Today, per-participant truth is split three ways: membership and *order* live in the auctions tab's comma-separated roster cell, claims live in the claims tab, and bid state lives in the bids tab. Every future per-person attribute — weights/shares, display-name-vs-pid for renames (the README spec wants the same table), a removed flag, someday a claim-token hash — belongs on one row per (auction, person). Keeping claims separate means weights would become a *fourth* parallel keyed-by-(aname, uname) table. One participants table normalizes all of it: a row is a seat; columns are the seat's attributes.

The under-appreciated payoff: it dissolves the CSV-concurrency problems. Several of the bugs we fought this week — the lock pile-up, the coalescing machinery, the stale-poll name loss — exist *because* roster edits are whole-list read-modify-write on one cell. With a participants table, the + row and × become row-level add/remove operations that are naturally commutative: two people adding different names can't clobber each other, and most of the client-side shielding (dirty windows, push coalescing) shrinks or disappears. The claim action already works this way; the roster should too.

What I'd deliberately not do: add the weight column now. Sheets reads are positional, so appending columns rightward later is backward-compatible and free — the table earns its keep from day one on structure, not speculative fields. Same for pid: it only pays when bids re-key by it, so it lands with the rename feature per the spec.

Cost and timing: this is a real change — Code.gs replaces the roster-CSV surgery (saveSettings, joinRoster) with row ops, getState derives roster and order from participant rows, the frontend's settings-push machinery simplifies, and the roster-mechanics quals get reworked. Call it a focused session. The argument for doing it *now* rather than when weights arrive: you just cleared the sheet, so schema churn is free — tabs regenerate on first touch — whereas later it's a migration. And claims-table → participants-table is a conversion, not a rewrite: the schema is literally today's claims schema; what changes is that a row comes to *mean* membership (created on add or walk-on bid, deleted on ×), with device as just one attribute.

So: same conclusion as your instinct, with the caveat that the win is mostly semantic consolidation and concurrency, and only secondarily "a place to put weights." Say the word and I'll build the participants migration as its own change.

keyed per-row node reuse? say more? how hard would it be to do this exquisitely correctly.
15:40 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 1m35s

It's the standard trick (the core of what React et al. do, hand-rolled at our scale): instead of replaceChildren-ing fresh rows every render, keep a map from uname → that row's living DOM node, and make render mean *reconcile*: create nodes for new unames, remove() nodes for vanished ones, and for survivors run an idempotent updateRow(node, state) that syncs classes, star glyph/disabled/tip, card-vs-slot-vs-editor content, subs, and × state — mutating the existing node rather than replacing it.

Why this kills the bug class outright: a click needs mousedown and mouseup on the same node, and focus/caret/IME live on node identity. Today any change-ful render (an op ack, another person's bid arriving) destroys every node, so gestures and focus only survive via workarounds — the fingerprint skip (no-op renders), the draft capture/restore (focus/caret), the wall-clock phase-lock (animations), and the test helpers' settled() waits. With reuse, the node under your finger persists through renders, so the whole class — including the op-ack variant we only dodged in the test helpers — is gone by construction, and the draft capture/restore machinery deletes (it becomes "don't write to a focused-or-dirty input," three lines, instead of capture-and-reinstate, twenty).

Why keying by uname is sound here: a row's uname never changes (it *is* the key), so the event listeners attached at creation — star, ×, form submit, all closing over uname — stay valid for the node's whole life. No listener churn, no leak (removed nodes take their listeners to GC). That's the property that makes this clean rather than fiddly.

The five genuinely subtle bits, i.e. where "exquisitely" lives:

  1. Idempotence of updateRow — same state in, same DOM out, regardless of the node's history. This is checkable by a property qual: render state A, mutate to B, back to A, and assert the node's outerHTML equals a freshly built row's (modulo the editor's live value). That one qual is worth more than any amount of reasoning.
  2. Editor no-clobber semantics — update value/defaultValue only when the input is neither focused nor dirty; leave selection alone always. Same predicate as today's draft capture, inverted and much smaller.
  3. Shimmer restart — re-adding .updated to a class that's already present doesn't restart a CSS animation, so two re-bids in consecutive renders would lose the second shimmer. Needs the classic remove-class → force reflow → re-add dance, exactly when the stamp changed and the class was already on.
  4. Reordering — moving an attached node (insertBefore) blurs it if focused. In practice our order is append-only (participants insertion order is stable; walk-ons append; re-adds append), so survivors essentially never move — but the reconciler should still do the correct general insertBefore walk rather than assume it.
  5. Content-type swaps inside the bid cell — editor↔card↔slot transitions replace that sub-tree; same-type updates mutate in place. Your own row transitioning is exactly the moment you might be typing, so this interacts with (2).

Effort and risk, honestly: renderStatus (~100 lines) refactors into buildRow (structure + listeners, once) + updateRow (sync) + a ~15-line keyed reconcile; call it 150 lines replacing 100, minus the deleted draft machinery. The fingerprint skip stays (skipping no-op work is still worth it; reuse makes the *change-ful* renders safe). A focused half-session to build, and most of the existing suite survives untouched since selectors don't change. New quals: the idempotence property above; node identity across a *change-ful* render (someone else's bid arrives, my row's node object persists); a real-Chrome story clicking a star while an add-op is in flight — which lets the settled() guards come out of the story helpers, un-papering what they papered over; focus surviving without the draft machinery (the existing 3h qual, passing for a better reason); and a rapid double re-bid still shimmering twice.

The main risk is completeness — forgetting one mutable facet (a tip string, a dataset attribute) so a row goes stale in some state. The property qual is the mitigation, since it diffs *entire* rows against fresh builds.

Recommendation: worth doing — it converts three workarounds into one mechanism and retires the last known interaction-eating race. Say the word and I'll build it red-first.

That report matches a real hole I can name: the freshness gate compares a poll's request time against the last write's *enqueue* time, but with serialized ops on a slow server, a snapshot requested after your last keystroke can still reflect only the ops that have landed so far — it gets adopted and wipes the not-yet-landed names until the final op's response restores them. Replicating deterministically as a qual first:

Twice green — 324 assertions. Updating memory:

Replicated, qual'd, fixed — 324 assertions green twice consecutively, 404 synced, frontend-only so no redeploy.

The mechanism, confirmed: your rapid adds queue as serialized ops behind real Apps Script latency (~1s each, so five names ≈ five seconds of pending writes). The freshness gate compared a poll's request time against the last write's *enqueue* time — but a snapshot requested after your last keystroke can still predate the later ops' *server commits*. That snapshot passed the gate, got adopted, and replaced your local roster with the partial one: every not-yet-landed name vanished, then reappeared when the final op's response painted. Exactly your symptom.

Replicating it took fixing the test harness first, which is the most interesting part: the fake fetch executed writes at *send* time, so the mock server was never mid-queue and the first version of my qual passed on the buggy code. The mock now snapshots reads at request time but commits writes at delivery time — like the real locked server working through its queue — and with that, your bug reproduced deterministically red. That fidelity fix hardens every future race qual, not just this one.

The fix is a stricter freshness discipline: writesPending counts every outstanding write (queued ops, bids, reveals) and writeSettledAt stamps each response's arrival. Reads are adopted only when no writes are pending *and* the read was requested at-or-after the last settle. Writes all funnel through one settleWrite: only the last write standing paints — directly when it's also the newest write, otherwise via a recovery fetch. Getting there surfaced two sub-bugs of my first attempt that the suite caught: out-of-order settles (a bid's response arriving while an older claim was pending) would have painted *nothing* until the next poll — the recovery fetch fixes that — and the recovery fetch itself got dropped by a same-millisecond timestamp tie, hence the >= with its reasoning in a comment.

One disclosed trade: while your own writes are pending, other people's updates don't paint (snapshots that interleave with your writes aren't trustworthy); that window is your ops' round-trip time, and the rare residual cases self-heal within one poll. Commit/push and version bump are yours.

what's the point of the line underlining the participant name when editing it? when you edit your bid it doesn't have a similar underline. maybe there's a reason? what do you think?
21:59 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 1m12s

There is a reason, and it's about what each field can afford, not a deliberate double standard. Every editable thing in the app signals focus somehow, but in the idiom its container allows:

  • Your bid editor is itself a full box (the dashed slot, or the green card), and on focus it gets the app's standard treatment: the 2px accent ring from the global input:focus rule ([style.css:104](style.css#L104)). It doesn't need an underline — the ring is its editing indicator.
  • The name field is a bare, borderless text fragment sitting *inside* a cell that already has its own border — and that cell also contains the star, and turns green once a bid is in. The standard accent ring there is ugly in every variant I tried: ring around just the 12ch fragment reads as a box-within-a-box; ring around the whole cell (the way the + row does it with :focus-within) falsely lassos the star into the edit, and clashes with the green has-bid border. So the ring is explicitly suppressed for names ([style.css:668](style.css#L668-L671)) and the underline is its quieter stand-in. Without it, the only cue that clicking did anything would be the blinking caret.

There's also a semantic nudge, though I'll admit it's secondary: the two fields have different commit rules. A bid draft is yours and persists — click away and your half-typed bid just sits there. A name edit is transactional — Enter commits, clicking away *discards*. The underline marks the field where you're "in" a volatile edit that will be thrown away unless you commit, which is the one place that state is worth flagging.

So: keep it, I'd say. If anything bothers me on re-inspection, it's that the underline is var(--muted) gray while every other focus signal in the app speaks accent — recoloring it var(--accent) would make "same color = focused, different shape per container" the consistent rule, at no extra noise. Happy to make that one-line change if you want it; leaving untouched for now.

12-for-12. Both threads closed — here's the full picture.

The underline (judgment exercised, no corners cut). Kept, and upgraded: it now speaks var(--accent) instead of muted gray, so the app has one consistent focus language — same color always means "focused," with the shape adapting to the container (ring for boxed inputs, underline for the bare name fragment where a ring would draw a box-in-a-box and lasso the star). I compared 1px against 2px in real screenshots: 2px reads heavier than the focus rings do relative to their boxes, so 1px stands. Verified in light and dark from first paint, on both plain and green has-bid cells, with a new story assert pinning that the focused name field's underline resolves to the accent color and the ring stays suppressed.

Your tooltip bug — diagnosis confirmed, and it was three bugs wearing one coat. The grayed controls dimmed themselves with opacity, and the tooltip is a ::before *inside* the control — so it inherited the dimming. Worse, opacity < 1 opens a CSS stacking context, which traps the tooltip's z-index inside the button and paints it *behind* every row that comes later in the DOM — both of your symptoms from one property. Carriers: the disabled × (your report), the dibsed star ("Too late to claim this is you" — same disease), and the padlock (whose filter: grayscale *also* creates a stacking context, and whose lockpulse transform would have done it a third way). The fix is what you proposed — control stays gray, tooltip normal: the × and star now dim via their color's alpha channel (color-mix), and the seal's graying and pulse moved onto its ::after glyph, so no tooltip host ever carries opacity, filter, or transform. Screenshot-verified: hovering the disabled × now shows a full-strength tip painted over the rows below. Three story asserts were retargeted to the new mechanism (same visual truths — glyph grayed, dibsed star dimmer, padlock pulses) plus two new ones red-first for the bug itself. One accepted leftover: while the app is busy, the whole ledger dims at the container level, tooltips included — consistent with everything being gray at that moment.

And the flake you saw fail mid-run ("ann row green") exposed a real hole in my settled() test helper from earlier today: when a claim op is queued right before a bid, the bid's response deliberately skips painting (a write is still pending) and the paint arrives via a recovery refresh *after* the busy flag clears — so waiting on busy alone wasn't enough. It now also waits out #status.stale, which is exactly "everything settled *and* painted." Twelve consecutive green runs after the fix.

Name collisions, thought through. The blunt truth: in a join-by-URL app, a "collision" and "joining" are the same physical act — you can't forbid one without breaking the other, and any name-based gate is theater given honor-system identity. The real risk is the *accidental* join: you name your auction "pizza" and land in a stranger's, discovering it only when their roster paints (which it does — that's the organic signal, but it arrives a beat late and gray). Strong yes on the intent split — typing is creating, link-following is joining. That inference matches how the app actually gets used (the share URL and QR code *are* the join mechanism; nobody joins a group auction by typing a name they guessed), and it kills the accidental-join foot-gun completely without touching the honor-system model. Two wrinkles and one refinement before it's buildable:

The wrinkle that matters: retyping to rejoin. People lose links and retype names they remember — "brunch" from their laptop, or the auction their friend said out loud. A hard "already exists, pick another" strands exactly those users, and their only workaround (edit the URL bar) is the thing non-savvy users never do. So I'd make the gate soft: typing an existing name doesn't silently drop you in, it tells you it exists and makes joining an explicit second action — one extra click, only in the collision case, and only for strangers.

The refinement: "exists" should mean "exists and shows no trace of you." We can recognize returning participants with data we already fetch: if the state's claims map contains your device id, or the roster holds your remembered name, it's plainly your auction — auto-join, no gate, so the common rejoin flow costs nothing. The gate then fires only on: *typed* name + *non-empty* auction + *no trace of you* — which is precisely the accidental collision (plus the rare "rejoining from a brand-new device" case, which pays one honest click). Note "exists" = has roster or bids; merely-visited names have no server rows at all, since typing never writes anything — creation is already lazy.

What stays true: following a link to a *nonexistent* auction still creates it, so you can share /brunch before touching it. And the simultaneous-creators race (two people type "pizza" in the same minute, both pass the check) is unfixable without reservations — they'll discover each other when rosters merge, which is rare and self-evident enough to accept.

One cost to name honestly: the aname field stops being a navigation box (its current tooltip literally says "or just edit the URL" — that stays the escape hatch for hopping to auctions you're not in). And the debounced switch means prefixes of existing names may flash the notice mid-typing, so the notice must be quiet and non-modal — a line by the field, not a banner.

Mechanically it's moderate: a "pending join" state (fetched but not adopted), the notice line with a join affordance, and quals for typed-vs-linked × empty-vs-occupied × trace-vs-stranger. If you want it, give me the notice copy ("Already exists — join it?" plus whatever the join affordance says), or I'll draft it in Latin per the house rule and you replace it.

Stories written, and they vindicated your original report more than your retraction — 398 assertions (91 gas + 189 frontend + 7 serve + 111 story), twice green, honest exits.

What you probably saw was real, three ways. Auditing the server against the stories exposed that claims were last-write-wins: saveClaim overwrote a held seat without complaint, so a machine with a stale screen (any page mid-poll-cycle shows alice as open for up to 5 seconds) could click her star and *silently steal* the registered claim — both machines then believe they're alice until the loser's next poll quietly unseats it. Two more doors beside it: an empty-device "release" was unverified, so anyone could evict anyone; and placeBid re-registered held seats to the bidder's device — a bid could hijack a seat outright. All three contradicted the claims system's own stated purpose.

The fix: first come, first served, refused loudly. A held seat now refuses a rival's claim with sedes iam occupata est (TODO "Someone already claimed that seat"); re-claiming your own seat stays idempotent (a device that lost localStorage re-latches); the radio behavior (your new claim releasing your old one) survives. Releasing is a new explicit release action that only the holder may perform — with the one graceful exception that releasing an *unheld* seat is a no-op, so soft self-claims release without drama. And a bid may never touch a seat someone else holds: deviceless bids from old clients count as nobody — fine on open seats, refused on held ones.

The stories, as requested — three, at two levels. Machine-level (jsdom, sections 2k/2l): *the alice race* — machine 1 claims, machine 2's stale screen still offers alice, machine 2 clicks, loses loudly (banner with the Latin), recovers to the dibsed truth on the recovery snapshot, and claims the open seat instead, while machine 1 never notices the skirmish; and *the stolen-seat bid* — machine 2 clicks and immediately types into the optimistic editor while its doomed claim is in flight, and both the claim and the bid bounce, with zero rows written. Human-level (real Chrome, Story 6, "two thumbs, one alice"): roommates on phones race for alice by tap, phone 2 loses loudly, takes bea, both bid, reveal by thumb — the whole arc.

Rule-6 disclosure, explicitly: two previously-pinned gas quals asserted the old semantics as features — "an empty device releases the claim" and "a device-less bid leaves claims alone." Both are rewritten to pin the refusals instead. If you want last-write-wins back (there's a defensible honor-system argument that anyone should be able to fix anyone's seat!), say so and I'll revert — but note the rename flow already covers the fix-someone's-typo use case without the stealing.

What stays by design: the soft self-claim window — a self-added name is local-only until your first bid registers it, so a name you typed for someone else is never locked against them. That window is probably the innocent thing you witnessed.

Deploy note: @17's cargo grows again (claim/release/bid seat semantics). Same instruction, now with more reason: npm run deploy and git push together.

  • ¶ / # — my favorite: while editing you see ¶ ("make it pretty"), while viewing you see # ("show me the source"). Each is the most iconic single glyph of its world — # is markdown's signature sigil, ¶ is typography's — both monochrome text that styles perfectly with the muted corner-whisper aesthetic, no emoji color clash.
  • ✎ / 👁 — edit-pencil and preview-eye: the most universally legible to people who've never heard of markdown, but the eye only exists as a color emoji (clashes), and the pencil-to-edit reads slightly wrong since you're *already* editing when it shows.
  • M↓ — the actual markdown logo mark as text; recognizable to insiders, cryptic to everyone else.
  • GitHub's convention is the words Write / Preview — the clearest of all but words, not symbols, and you wanted subtle.

What happens on deploys:

The only thing the script ever creates is a fresh tab (with headers) when one doesn't exist — the same first-use behavior it's always had. Fixed — geography is now looked up once a week instead of once per page load. Suite twice green at 458 (107 gas + 226 frontend + 7 serve + 118 story).

Why you were seeing it: locate() fired on every page load, and your dev loop is Live-Server-style — every file save reloads the page, so every save was another ipwho.is request from your IP. A day of editing burned through their free rate window, hence the 429s. So yes, effectively dev-specific: real users load once per visit and would essentially never hit it.

The fix: locate() now caches the result in localStorage (tauction-geo plus a tauction-geo-at date stamp, TTL one week — [app.js:114](app.js#L109-L131)). Fresh cache means no network request at all; stale or missing means fetch and re-stamp; a failed lookup stays quiet and uncached so the next load retries. Two ifs added and disclosed: the cache-freshness check, and the no-luck early return (which existed before as the r.city && guard).

One caveat: browsers print failed-request console lines no matter what the code does, so while their rate limit still has you blocked you may see one more 429 on the next cold load — the cache can't seed until a request succeeds. Once one goes through, that's the last lookup for a week.

Quals (written red-first, watched fail, then implemented): first load fetches once and stamps the dated cache; a page seeded with a fresh cache makes zero lookups *and* provably uses the cached value — its bid registers a claim whose server-side blurb ends "in Rainbow City, AL", the seeded city; an 8-day-old stamp refetches and re-stamps.

Options, roughly in order of fit: y-webrtc (peers sync directly; only a lightweight public signaling server involved; the sheet stays as commit-level persistence — closest to the no-server ethos), a tiny hosted relay (y-websocket on a free-tier dyno — a real server to run, against the grain here), or a hosted service like Liveblocks/PartyKit (easy, but a paid dependency). So: yes, Chrome caching old CSS was entirely possible — in three distinct ways — and hunting it flushed out two zombie servers besides. Twice green at 524 (117 gas + 275 frontend + 8 serve + 124 story).

The three caching layers, worst to mildest:

  1. Local dev was the sneaky one, now fixed: serve.py sent no Cache-Control, so Chrome applied *heuristic* caching — roughly 10% of a file's age since last-modified. A style.css untouched for ten hours could be served an hour stale on plain navigations (F5 revalidates; typing the URL doesn't). serve.py now sends no-store on everything — a dev server must never lie about freshness — with a serve-qual pinning the header.
  2. Production (you pushed, by the way — live style.css is stamped today 04:20 UTC): GitHub Pages serves max-age=600, so up to ten minutes of staleness after any push, browser and installed app alike. Accepted; hard-reload when eyeballing a fresh deploy.
  3. The installed Android app specifically: same HTTP cache, plus Chrome re-checks WebAPK *manifests* on a lazy multi-day schedule — so the gavel icon may take days to reach an already-installed app, or a reinstall to force it.

The bonus catch: while pinning the no-store header, the qual "failed" — because a *crashed run's leftover serve.py* was squatting the qual port, silently winning the EADDRINUSE race and serving pre-fix bytes. The suite was interrogating a zombie. Both qual suites now pre-flight their port and fail loudly with lsof instructions if anything answers before the spawn — and that guard caught a *second* zombie on the story port on its very first run. Two stale servers had been sitting there able to poison any suite run with old code; that class is now closed too.

Paste A — the deep refresh (nukes CacheStorage and any service worker, re-fetches every loaded asset straight from the network updating the HTTP cache, then reloads — this is stronger than ⌘⇧R, which bypasses but doesn't *replace* cached entries):

(async () => {
  if (window.caches) for (const k of await caches.keys()) await caches.delete(k);
  if (navigator.serviceWorker) for (const r of await navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistrations()) await r.unregister();
  await Promise.all(performance.getEntriesByType('resource').map(e => fetch(e.name, { cache: 'reload' }).catch(() => {})));
  await fetch(location.href, { cache: 'reload' });
  location.reload();
})();

Paste B — the verdict printer (run after A settles; tells us decisively whether the browser has the fix and what ink it's actually computing):

  2. The open tip now live-updates: the old content: attr() tip re-rendered when state changed under your cursor; the event-driven singleton showed stale text until the pointer moved. Re-pinned honestly (seal hover with the banner standing), with both heights also enforced by the z-ladder registry. 02:31 Claude Code claude-fable-5 thought for 49s

Short answer: not with the current URL scheme — and the blocker is a status code, not the meta tags. The OG card *is* in every byte of what /someauction serves (404.html is index.html verbatim) — but GitHub Pages serves it with HTTP 404, and the major unfurlers (Slack, iMessage, WhatsApp, X) refuse to build cards from non-200 responses. That's the same 404-fallback hack that makes /slug work at all: pretty paths and crawler-visible auction URLs are structurally at odds on static Pages. Root gets a card because root is a real 200.

Three ways out, and it's your aesthetic to rule on:

  1. Accept root-only previews — status quo, zero change. Shared auction links unfurl nowhere important.
  2. Switch the canonical URL to a query form — tauction.dreev.es/?chores — which fetches / (a real 200) for every auction, so every shared link previews. Big bonus: the entire 404 apparatus becomes deletable — 404.html, sync-404, the byte-copy qual, serve.py's fallback handler, the whole edit-one-file-ship-two hazard. Big cost: your /chores URLs, which you chose deliberately ("the URL bar itself names the auction"), become /?chores — and old shared /slug links need a legacy shim (either keep the 404 fallback for them, or the redirect machinery you originally refused).
  3. Hybrid — path URLs stay canonical, but the *share button* hands out the ? form. New shares preview; old links and pretty typing keep working; nothing gets deleted. Two URL forms forever, which is its own smell, but it's a five-line change with no migration.

My take: 3 gets you what you actually asked for (previews on shared auction links — the links that *matter* are the shared ones, and the share button already owns those) at trivial cost, and leaves 2 available later if the two-forms smell bothers you more than /?chores does. But /slug vs /?slug is exactly the kind of taste call you've overruled me on before, so: pick, and I'll build it with the usual red-first treatment.

Leave it alone. Recommendation with reasoning:

The cold-page window is narrower than it first looks. Walking the real arrival paths:

  1. Creating an auction goes through switchAuction, which ingests the probe response before the field even unlocks — state is never null there.
  2. Returning to an auction paints from the localStorage cache instantly — not null either.
  3. The only null window is first-ever visit by URL, and only until the first fetch lands (~0.5–2s). To hit it you have to read a page you've never seen, decide on a name, and commit it inside that window.

And the behavior in that window is now honest rather than broken: queueOp adds .stale before the if (state) gate, so the moment you commit the name the box grays and the gavel hammers — the app's standard busy signal — and the row lands with the add's own response. That's "stale means busy" working as designed, just for one extra round trip.

Against that, the fix would cost real complexity. Making state never-null via a synthetic empty snapshot poisons two latches: descModeSet would choose edit-mode from the synthetic blank and then hold a real arriving blurb in source view, and wasRevealed would latch false off the synthetic render, so a cold visitor who typed into an already-revealed auction gets a false confetti ceremony. Both are fixable, but each fix is a new flag or conditional — trading a ~1-second cosmetic delay on a rare path for two subtler state-machine hazards on paths the quals currently pin hard. That fails the Pareto test: it's not a dominating move, it's a trade, and a bad one.

So: ship what's here (it's all client-side — no Code.gs deploy needed, just your commit/push; the version span is already bumped to v2026.07.18-b). If the deferred paint ever bothers you in practice, the right follow-up is the full rethink — make the empty state a first-class representable state, with descModeSet re-keyed to the first unstale render and the fanfare latch made explicit — done as its own change with its own quals, not bolted onto this one.

  • The naive fix — split on code spans and transform only the text between — silently breaks [`y`](url) , a code span *labeling* a link, which works today. The stash approach preserves it, and the qual now pins that preservation explicitly.
  • The placeholder <<n>> is unforgeable by construction rather than by luck: the escape pass has already converted every author-typed < to &lt;, so no input can counterfeit one, and no emitted tag ever produces two < in a row. The fun piece: a fuzz battery for mdRender

New qual 2p4: 500 deterministic rounds of adversarial markdown soup — half-open syntax, nested markers, hostile HTML, javascript: links, and a forged <<0>> aimed at the new placeholder mechanism — asserting the renderer's promises under fire: never throws, pure function, only whitelisted tags materialize, attributes only on <a> (href http(s)-only), no placeholder leaks, no markup inside code spans. Seeded PRNG, so a failure is a *permanent* replicata: the assertion label prints the exact offending input.

Then I verified the battery itself, twice over, in a scratchpad harness:

  • Teeth: ran the identical soup against app.js with the pre-fix inline surgically restored — the battery catches it, auto-generating a monstrous minimal-ish replicata string.
  • Vacuity: tallying which tags actually materialized revealed that random soup had *never once assembled a valid link* — the entire <a> invariant set was passing vacuously (and <h3> never appeared either). Fixed by adding whole-link tokens (one of them code-labeled, so the trickiest composition is under fire too) — <a> now materializes 470 times per run — and the qual now enforces a coverage floor: every whitelisted tag must appear at least once, so the battery can pass vacuously exactly never, and deterministically can't flake.

13:02 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 1m32s · 1m34s wall-clock time

Timezone audit — let me sweep every timestamp path in the system before answering.

Yes — the right thing is happening, and it's happening for a clean architectural reason: there is exactly one clock in this system. Every stamp — tini, tmod, tfin, tblurb, tbid — is minted server-side by new Date().toISOString(), always UTC, always the fixed 24-char YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ shape (and Apps Script's toISOString ignores the script's timezone setting, so the sheet's locale can't leak in). The three layers each do the correct thing:

Comparing — the two load-bearing comparisons are r[3] > tfin (is this bid row at-or-before the gavel) and the tblurb compare-and-swap. Both compare server-minted stamps against server-minted stamps: same clock, same format, and fixed-width ISO-UTC compares lexicographically exactly as it compares chronologically. No client clock ever participates in an ordering decision — the client's write-adoption logic (lastWriteAt, writeSettledAt, started >=) compares Date.now() only against other Date.now() values from the same machine.

Displaying — the only two places server time meets a viewer's eyes both handle zones deliberately. closedStamp renders tfin via getHours/getDate etc., i.e. the viewer's local wall clock (the comment says "in the viewer's local time" — that's the spec), and DST is free because the browser does that mapping. ago() subtracts Date.parse(iso) — zone-independent for ISO-with-Z — from the client clock, and the one place skew *could* show (a client behind the server seeing a bid "submitted -3s ago") is already floored to 0s with a comment saying exactly why.

The geo cache TTL is client-ISO vs client-now — self-consistent.

Three findings from the audit, all assessment, none fixed:

  1. The Closed line carries no zone marker. Two participants in different zones will see different wall-clock text for the same instant — "Closed 2026-07-16 13:01 Thu" vs "…16:01 Thu". That's inherent to the local-time spec and right for a screen; it only bites if someone screenshots the line into a group chat as if it were canonical. Your call whether that ever matters.
  1. The whole edifice rests on stamps staying TEXT in the sheet, and the armor has a known edge. The '@' plain-text format is applied at tab creation to getMaxRows() rows (1000). If a stamp cell ever escapes that — row 1001+, or someone hand-clearing formats — Sheets coerces the ISO string to a real date, and rows()'s String() then yields "Fri Jul 17 2026 18:23:45 GMT-0700 (Pacific Daylight Time)" in the *script's* timezone. I verified the nasty part empirically: that string sneaks past ingest's tfin.includes('T') assert — "GMT" and "Time" both contain a T — and it misorders lexicographically against ISO, so the standing-bid-at-or-before-tfin logic would silently misjudge rather than fail loudly. If you want the belt: tighten the assert to a real shape check (/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/) so a coerced stamp crashes the ingest instead of rendering nonsense — one-line change plus a qual, on the anti-Postel doctrine. Say the word.
  1. Minor, already flagged in turn one: a legacy bid row with a blank tbid (the hand-written-row case the gas quals bless) makes ago('') return "NaNd", so the tooltip reads "bid submitted NaNd ago" — time-adjacent cosmetic on a tamper-only path.

Two questions — let me answer the format cliff properly, and actually test the ipwho.is theory from your machine (same public IP as your browser) before speculating:

Both answered — and the live probe just explained your 429 mystery rather neatly.

The format cliff, concretely

Google Sheets cells default to "Automatic" format, which means Sheets *interprets* whatever gets written: 007 becomes the number 7, MAR1 becomes March 1st, and an ISO stamp like 2026-07-18T22:01:33.510Z becomes a real datetime value. Code.gs defends against this — that's why a bid of "007" stays "007" — by setting the cells to plain-text (setNumberFormat('@')) when it first creates a tab. The catch: that armor is applied to getMaxRows() rows *at creation time*, and a fresh sheet's grid is 1000 rows. The bids tab is an append-only log across all auctions combined, so its row count only grows. If appendRow ever writes row 1001, that row sits outside the armored range — and if the cell is Automatic, the ISO stamp gets coerced into a datetime, which reads back through String() as "Fri Jul 18 2026 15:01:33 GMT-0700 (…)". That breaks the lexicographic standing-bid-versus-tfin comparison, and bid text like "007" quietly becomes "7". Since yesterday's STAMP_RE work the client at least refuses such a payload *loudly* instead of rendering nonsense — but that's still an outage starting at submission #1001.

The honest caveat: it's a *suspected* cliff. Sheets often inherits formatting from the row above when appendRow grows the grid, in which case row 1001 arrives pre-armored and this never fires. I didn't want to claim it as a confirmed bug without testing against real Sheets. The fix-shape if you want certainty: armor whole columns (or re-arm on growth) in tab(), plus a one-time live test — small Code.gs change, needs a deploy.

The ipwho.is 429s — probed live from this machine (your IP)

Findings: a plain request right now returns 200, success:true — and here's the good part — with cf-cache-status: HIT. Adding an Origin: https://tauction.dreev.es header (what your browser's CORS fetch sends) flips it to cf-cache-status: BYPASS: browser requests from the app bypass Cloudflare's cache and hit the counted, rate-limited API, while plain navigations often get free cached rides. That's why ipwho.is "works in your normal browser" while the app sees 429s — they're not even taking the same path.

As for why you *keep* seeing them: it's the failure-retry spiral. locate() only stamps its localStorage cache on success, so during any throttled window every page load retries and logs a fresh 429 to the console — and dev live-reload means a load per file save, which both sustains the spam and is what likely trips the burst limit in the first place. Each origin and browser profile has its own localStorage too (localhost:8000, tauction.dreev.es, your phone, every incognito window), so each needs one successful lookup to go quiet. A 4-request burst just now got all 200s, so your IP isn't currently exhausted — the 429s you see are transient throttling during exactly the sessions where you'd be looking at the console.

Recommendation: no fallback service. Geography is decoration by your own doctrine; a second geo provider is a new dependency and one more party seeing your users' IPs, to slightly improve tooltip garnish availability — a trade, not a Pareto move. Steady state with the day-cache is ~1 lookup per browser per day, which the free tier covers hundreds of times over. What *would* help is small and dependency-free: stamp the attempt, not just the success, so a failed lookup waits out a backoff (say an hour) instead of retrying on every load — that kills the console spam and the burst-limit feedback loop in one line-ish change, and the failure path isn't pinned by any qual, so it's free to change. Want me to do that one?

The format cliff, worked all the way to ground

The clearest way to say it, in three beats:

  1. Why armor exists. Sheets *interprets* anything written into a cell unless that cell is formatted plain-text. This app writes strings: bids like 007, stamps like 2026-07-18T22:01:33.510Z. In an interpreting cell, Sheets stores the number 7 and a real datetime — and reading those back gives "7" and "Fri Jul 18 2026 15:01:33 GMT-0700 (…)". The first corrupts bid text; the second breaks the lexicographic stamp ordering that decides which bid beat the gavel.
  2. The armor's extent. tab() applies plain-text format exactly once, at tab creation, to getMaxRows() rows — and a fresh sheet's grid is 1000 rows. Rows 1–1000 are safe forever. Think of it as a paint job applied to the parking lot as originally built.
  3. The cliff. The bids tab is an append-only log across *all* auctions, so it only grows. Writing row 1001 forces Sheets to first *grow the grid* — and whether newborn grid rows inherit the plain-text format from the rows above, or arrive in default interpreting mode, is the whole question.

What research settles: the Apps Script docs are silent, but the REST API underneath has exactly two grow primitives — insertDimension, which has an inheritFromBefore flag and *can* copy formatting from the row above, and appendDimension, which appends blank rows with default properties, no inheritance. Which one appendRow uses when it grows the grid is undocumented. Community evidence leans "no inheritance": there's an entire genre of workaround scripts and support threads about appended rows (Google Forms responses being the classic case) failing to keep the formatting of the rows above them. So the right posture is: treat the cliff as real — and even if today's behavior happened to inherit, it's undocumented behavior that could change underneath us, which is its own reason not to lean on it.

Urgency, measured against your live sheet (it's link-readable, so I counted): bids 17 rows, users 11, auctions 8. The fastest-growing tab is ~983 submissions from the edge — years away at current usage — and since the STAMP_RE work, falling off it would be a loud "bad state shape" banner, not silent corruption.

  • The belt (recommended): make the question moot. A tiny Code.gs helper: appendRow, then re-apply '@' to the just-written row and re-set the same values — the rewrite un-coerces anything a transiently-interpreting cell mangled, all inside the script lock so no reader ever sees the intermediate. Costs two extra Sheets calls per write (~100–200ms on a 0.5–2s baseline), immune to whatever Sheets does, forever. The arrival edge

The three one-shot latches — caretPlaced, descModeSet, and wasRevealed's null sentinel — turned out to all fire on the *same event*: the first adopted snapshot, cached or live. So they're now one named thing: adopted, the arrival edge. The caret lands on the arrival render, the description picks its mode on the arrival render, and fanfare belongs only to a *witnessed* sealed→revealed flip — a latecomer's arrival sets the baseline silently. switchAuction resets one bit instead of three, and the null-sentinel pattern is gone (wasRevealed is a plain boolean now).

Per the refactor discipline, the net went up before the wire moved: two characterization pins for arrival behaviors that were previously unpinned — a stale-unrevealed cache makes your arrival a *witnessed* reveal (fanfare and money play, at the strike's usual beat), and a cache-painted arrival seats the caret before the live fetch even lands. Both were green against the old code, stayed green through the fold, and one of them caught its own timing bug on the way in (asserting confetti before the 850ms strike), which is exactly the kind of thing I now distrust by default after yesterday's tautology sweep.

The commit pulse (your ruling: brief flash)

The instant a gesture queues a write, the field it happened in glows the shimmer green once and fades (~0.6s) — the outgoing twin of the incoming shimmer: sweep means *their news arrived*, glow means *yours is away*. It fires in five places: the auction name (only when the name actually takes — a gate refusal stays pulseless beside its banner), the + row (any add or seat-claim), the bid editor (at submit, not at settle), renames (a same-name snap-back doesn't pulse), and the description card. The sticky banner (your ruling: sticky + ×)

The 5-second self-destruct is deleted. A banner now leaves exactly three ways: its own × (new, quiet, inked like the message), a newer banner replacing it, or a later *successful* settle retiring it — stale bad news doesn't outlive the problem it reported, while the durable signal (the red field) stays. The dead-end sign's special "sticky" status is gone because *all* banners are sticky now; what remains of that function is just the markup-vs-text distinction, renamed linkBanner.

good idea. what are the pros and cons of polling in the background?
09:11 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 57s

Let me check the actual poll cadence first so the numbers are right.

Here's my honest read, for this app specifically (5s poll, Apps Script backend).

Pros

  • The tab-title payoff completes: 🔒→🎉 happens in the tab bar while you're elsewhere, which is exactly when you'd want it — "waiting on the gavel" is the one state where you've parked the tab and moved on.
  • Returning to a tab shows current truth instead of up-to-5s-stale (though there's a much cheaper way to get this one — see below).
  • Fresher state in forgotten tabs means fewer stale-roster races losing to the server (the loud refusals Sol just added would fire less often).

Cons

  • The backend is quota-bound and executes as you. Every poll is a doGet execution against your account's Apps Script quotas — shared across all visitors, roughly 0.5–2s of runtime each. One tab left open 24h at 5s cadence is ~17,000 requests and hours of accumulated runtime per day. Tabs get forgotten; that cost is perpetual and multiplies per tab, and dead tabs' polls compete with live bidders' writes for the 30-simultaneous-executions ceiling and the script lock during actual games.
  • Browsers won't actually let you poll at 5s in the background. Chrome's intensive throttling clamps background timers to about once per minute after a few minutes; Safari and mobile browsers freeze or discard background pages outright (and the PWA-on-a-phone case — your hallway audience — is the most aggressively frozen of all). So the honest deliverable isn't "flips within 5s," it's "flips within a minute, sometimes, on desktop." A feature that silently degrades like that is anti-Postel-adjacent: it makes a promise the platform won't keep.
  • Battery and radio cost on phones, for a payoff (one bit: revealed or not) that arrives at most once per auction's lifetime. Continuous cost, rare benefit.

The middle path that gets most of the value for ~none of the cost: refresh once on visibilitychange → visible. No background traffic at all, but the moment you click back to a tab it's current immediately instead of waiting out the interval. That kills the practical staleness complaint; the only thing it doesn't deliver is the 🎉 flipping while the tab is unfocused. If you wanted that too, the bounded version is: poll in the background *only* while the auction is hot (all bids in, awaiting reveal) at the browser's throttled cadence — the flip lands within a minute during the only window it can happen, and forgotten tabs of finished or idle auctions stay silent. That costs one condition, which per house rules I'd want your ruling on anyway.

My recommendation: visibilitychange refresh yes, unconditional background polling no. The hot-window variant is defensible if the tab-bar reveal moment matters to you enough to spend a branch on it.

what do you mean "the only window it can happen"? if not everyone has bid, but then they do bid, how do we know that without polling?
09:36 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 58s

You're right, and that's a real hole in what I proposed — thanks for pressing on it. The gate I described evaluates on the tab's *last-seen* state, and a backgrounded tab's knowledge freezes at its final visible poll. So if bids were still missing when you switched away, the tab sits in "not hot, don't poll" — and since not-polling is exactly what keeps it ignorant, it never learns the last bid landed, never enters the "hot window," and never sees the reveal. The gate only works in the case where everyone had already bid before you backgrounded the tab. That's the least common waiting scenario, not the main one — usually *you've* bid and you're waiting on stragglers, which is precisely the state my gate would go blind in.

The general principle I tripped over: a background-polling gate has to fail open, not closed. If the gate errs toward polling, one wasted poll discovers the truth and self-corrects. If it errs toward silence, the blindness is self-perpetuating, because polling is the only way the gate's own inputs get refreshed.

That asymmetry is also why there's exactly one clean state-based gate available: revealed. It's a one-way latch, and the tab learns it *by* polling — so "poll in background unless revealed" errs only on the polling side (a revealed-elsewhere tab polls once more, sees the latch, and goes permanently quiet). The corrected menu is really just:

  1. No background polling — the title updates next time you look (plus a visibilitychange refresh so "next time you look" is instant). Zero background cost, no reveal-while-away flip.
  2. Poll in background whenever unrevealed, stopping forever at reveal. This is the coherent version of what I was reaching for. The browser throttles it to roughly once a minute on desktop and freezes it on mobile regardless, so the real cost is ~1,400 requests/day per *abandoned unrevealed* desktop tab — the finished-auction tabs, which are the ones people most often leave open forever, cost nothing after their one discovery poll.
  3. Time-decay schemes (poll for a while after backgrounding, then give up) — bounds the abandoned-tab cost but adds machinery and a mushy promise ("flips if it happens within an hour"). I'd rule it out on house style alone.

So the honest trade is between 1 and 2, and it's the question of whether the 🎉-while-away flip is worth ~1/min from every open unrevealed tab. My lean is still 1 — the flip is a nicety, the visibilitychange refresh captures most of the felt value, and the backend runs on your quota — but 2 is now the version I'd defend if you want the tab bar to announce the gavel.

The central omission is emerging: the current title has only “sealed” and “revealed,” while the auction itself has a third, operationally important state—“all bids are in; someone must press reveal.” I’m checking the exact state derivation and whether background reads carry that signal cleanly.

Fable fixed the self-blinding “hot window” mistake, but it still treats a background poll as if it only updates the title. In this app it does much more.

  1. A hidden poll would perform a full render.

[refresh()](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:273) calls ingest() and render(). If reveal arrives while hidden, that:

  • Consumes the one-shot gavel/confetti ceremony offscreen via [celebrate()](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:473).
  • Consumes incoming-bid shimmers.
  • Can disable a focused dirty bid/name field, whose blur handler may then submit the draft after the gavel and produce an error ([bid blur](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:741), [reveal disabling](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:816)).
  • Can create a sticky network-error banner while hidden; later successful reads do not clear it.

A hidden poll therefore needs a title-only/pending-state path, or an explicit ruling that hidden tabs count as witnessing the reveal.

  1. It misses the state that actually calls the user back.

There are three states, not two:

waiting → ready for someone to reveal → revealed

Reveal is deliberately manual ([Code.gs](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/apps-script/Code.gs:438)), and readiness is already derived separately ([app.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:480)). But the title stays 🔒 for both waiting and ready ([stringles.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/stringles.js:51)). Background polling can learn that the last bid arrived yet communicate nothing. The first product question is whether the away-signal means “come back and reveal” or “someone revealed.” If it is the former, the title needs a third state.

  1. Its timer arithmetic is Chrome-specific.

Chrome only moves chained timers to approximately once per minute after more than five minutes hidden and under additional conditions. Firefox Desktop’s documented minimum is one second, so tauction’s five-second interval may remain a five-second interval—about 17,000 calls/day. Chrome’s policy, cross-browser timer behavior.

If background polling is chosen, tauction should request an explicit coarse hidden cadence, such as 60 seconds, rather than outsourcing its traffic ceiling to browser heuristics.

  1. The backend analysis is partly wrong.

State GETs do not acquire the script lock; only mutations do ([Code.gs](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/apps-script/Code.gs:128)). Polls consume execution and Sheets capacity, but do not “compete for the script lock.” Because reads are unlocked, they can instead observe intermediate states during multi-write mutations.

Also, every poll reads and scans the complete auctions, users, and append-only bids tabs ([Code.gs](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/apps-script/Code.gs:265)). Cost therefore grows with all historical activity. The repository’s own live measurement says 1.6–3.0 seconds for a bare state GET ([gas-quals.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/quals/gas-quals.js:779)), not Fable’s 0.5–2 seconds.

The general quota concern is valid, but Google’s published 90-minute/6-hour daily runtime quota is specifically trigger runtime; the documented general limits include 30 simultaneous executions per user and 1,000 per script. Apps Script quotas.

  1. “Immediate on visibilitychange” overpromises.

It would start revalidation immediately, but the old controls remain actionable until the request finishes. Furthermore, [refresh()](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:273) silently refuses while another fetch is active, has no timeout, and queues no refire. Preventing stale-return races would also require visibly graying/locking the ledger until catch-up completes.

Recommendation: retain no hidden polling if the goal is merely freshness on return; add visibility-triggered revalidation and gray the stale UI. If the tab itself should signal progress while away, use an explicit slow hidden cadence, add the ready state to the title, update only title/pending state while hidden, and defer the full render and ceremony until visible. “Stop at reveal” should apply only to hidden polling, since descriptions remain editable after reveal. No files changed.

The principled case, per the links:

  • Anti-Postel doesn't apply — it's about rejecting malformed *input*. This input is well-formed and the requested post-condition ("alice is on the roster") already holds. Reporting failure for a satisfied request is the actual falsehood; that's your complaint exactly.

Let me trace the actual mechanics before diagnosing — the device id minting, the claim flow, and how each browser decides what bid text to show.

Traced it. Nothing is fubar in the data — the sheet has exactly one standing bid for bob (the log is append-only; the latest row at reveal wins). What's fubar is that both browsers *display* a different "bob's bid," and at most one of them is telling the truth. Here's the full chain:

The deviceID guess is wrong, in a good way. Each browser profile mints crypto.randomUUID() into localStorage on first load ([app.js:155-158](app.js#L155-L158)) — incognito has separate storage, so it has its *own* uuid. The architecture is already what you describe as right. That's also why the two-normal-tabs test behaves: two tabs of one profile are literally one device — same uuid, same tauction-pids, same tauction-mybids — so an edit in one tab is read back by the other on its next poll.

The takeover is not a malfunction — it's the faire ruling. Until 2026-07-21 the server refused a claim on a seat held by another device (ERROR1304 seatHeldCopy). That lock was deliberately deleted in the faire fix, because Safari re-minted her uuid and her own seat refused her: claims became "consistency markers, not auth — a tap on a taken star TAKES the seat, last write wins" ([Code.gs:631-638](apps-script/Code.gs#L631-L638), [app.js:980-987](app.js#L980-L987)). Your expectata is exactly the pre-faire behavior; the regression is that ruling's known cost surfacing.

Why each window sees its own bid. Sealed bid text never leaves the server, so each browser renders a bid it placed from its own tauction-mybids memory ([app.js:574-587](app.js#L574-L587)) — "you always see the bids your own browser placed." That rule is only truthful while one browser sits in a seat. After incognito takes bob and re-bids, the normal window is unseated (a rival's registered claim demotes mypid() to nobody, [app.js:562-567](app.js#L562-L567)), and bob's row becomes a card showing the normal window's *superseded* text — stamp and stack sheets update, but the words silently stay stale. Incognito's editor shows its own text. Two windows, two "bob's bids," one lie.

Two ways out, and they pull against each other:

  1. Bid protects its seat from claims too — the server already refuses removing a bidder; extend the same refusal to claiming a seat that has a bid. Simple, matches your expectata. Cost: re-creates a slice of faire — a bidder whose localStorage evaporates (Safari ITP does this) can never re-enter their own seat to re-bid, and there's no escape hatch short of the claim tokens the spec already rejected.
  2. Keep takeovers, stop the display lying — stamp the local bid memory with bcount at placement; when the seat's current bcount no longer matches, this browser's text is superseded, so render the masked decoy like any other sealed bid (and optionally banner the unseating instead of demoting silently). Honor system intact, faire intact, and every window shows something true.

Which way do you want it?

10:48 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 1m8s

I think the faire ruling was half right, and the half that's wrong isn't the half you're pointing at.

The claim lock that refused faire wasn't anti-Postel virtue — it was an if-statement enforcing a credential the system doesn't have. A deviceID is an unstable uuid (Safari purges localStorage on its own schedule) that sits in a link-visible sheet, so the lock couldn't stop anyone acting in bad faith — they can read the uuid right out of the sheet and send it. A lock that can't stop adversaries but permanently strands honest users with cleared storage is theater, and "clearer errors" can't rescue it: the clearest possible message to faire would still have been a refusal with no path forward, because her old uuid was gone from the universe. There's no wording that fixes a dead end. Deleting that lock was the anti-magic move — one rule (last write wins), no recovery flows, no escape hatches, consistent with "honor system throughout" everywhere else in the app.

What the ruling got wrong is that it deleted the refusal without adding the loudness. Anti-Postel doesn't demand the server refuse things; it demands nothing fail *silently*. Two silences slipped through:

  1. The display lies. The unseated window keeps rendering its cached text as if it were bob's standing bid. That's Postel-style tolerance of divergence — the client "helpfully" shows what it remembers instead of admitting it no longer knows. The echo design is the anti-Postel fix: render only what the server attests, mask the rest. Notably, this is needed under *either* claim policy — even if you restored a lock, the API takes bids by pid (honor system), so a rival re-bid and a stale cache stay representable. The lock doesn't subsume it.
  2. The unseating is mute. When a rival claim demotes you, your editor quietly becomes a card mid-session. That deserves a banner in the unseated window — the event announced, not refused.

So my actual position: takeovers stay legal (the lock was fake anyway), the display becomes incapable of lying (echo, cache deleted), and the takeover becomes loud (banner for the unseated, and the taken star's tip already names the claimant's rig for the taker). Faire under this regime: no refusals, and if someone re-bids her seat while she's away, she comes back to a masked card and a banner instead of a phantom of her old bid.

The one real fork left is whether you want *bid finality per device* — "once bob bids from browser X, only browser X may revise it." That's a product stance, not an engineering one, and it contradicts "everything stays editable, honor system" as written. If you want it anyway, it's the refuse-claims-on-bid-seats variant, plus the echo fix regardless. Do you?
